hints: Look for the curve that shoots up very sharply from near 0 to about 20 kPa. Which arrow is pointing right at the top of that big, tall peak?
Remember that ventricular systole means the thick ventricle muscle contracts hard, so ventricular pressure must rise suddenly to push blood out into the aorta.
walkthrough:
**Identify the three pressure curves**

First, let's read the graph like a story. The tiny dotted line near the bottom is atrial pressure, it only reaches about 1 to 2 kPa.

The dashed line that jumps from near 0 up to about $20 \text{ kPa}$ is ventricular pressure. The solid line that stays high around $12$ to $20 \text{ kPa}$ is pressure in the aorta.

**Recall what ventricular systole does**

Ventricular systole is contraction of the ventricles. When the muscle squeezes, pressure inside the ventricle rises very fast and very high.

That high pressure closes the atrioventricular valves and opens the semilunar valves, so blood is forced out into the arteries:
$$\text{ventricular pressure} > \text{atrial pressure and aortic pressure (briefly)}$$

**Match the arrows to the events**

Arrow B points to the flat top of the tall dashed peak at about $0.3$ to $0.4 \text{ s}$. That is exactly when ventricular pressure is highest during contraction.

So B must be ventricular systole, the powerful squeeze that ejects blood.

options.A: Arrow A points to the small low bump in atrial pressure before the big rise. That is atrial systole, not ventricular systole.
options.B: Arrow B points to the peak of ventricular pressure at about 20 kPa. This high plateau is caused by strong ventricular contraction, so it is ventricular systole.
options.C: Arrow C points to the low, flat period when ventricular pressure is near 0 kPa. That is ventricular diastole when the ventricle is relaxed and filling.
options.D: Arrow D points to the solid aortic line with its small second bump. That is aortic pressure during diastole with elastic recoil, not ventricular contraction.
